blocks.prompt: The Crab That Wears a Borrowed Shell
blocks.text: A hermit crab is born without a shell to call its own. The front of its body is hard, like armor. The back of its body is soft and curls to one side. That soft part would make an easy snack, so the crab hides it inside an empty snail shell. The crab backs in. Then it pulls its big claw across the opening like a lid. Now nothing can get in. A hermit crab grows, but its shell does not grow with it. So one day the shell feels too tight. The crab must find a bigger one, hop out, and slip into the new home fast.

blocks.prompt: The Line for a Better House
blocks.text: A hermit crab is not really a crab, not the way a blue crab is. Its front half wears hard armor, but its back half is soft, bare, and curled in a spiral. A hungry fish could end that crab in one bite. So the hermit crab does something clever. It finds an empty snail shell and backs into it. The spiral of its body fits the spiral of the shell. Now the crab has armor it never had to grow. There is one problem. The crab keeps getting bigger. The shell does not. Every so often the crab has to trade up, and good empty shells are hard to find. So hermit crabs wait. When a fine big shell washes ashore, crabs gather around it. They sort themselves into a line by size, biggest at the front, smallest at the back. The biggest crab climbs into the new shell. The next crab takes the shell it left behind. Then the next, and the next. In a few seconds, the whole line has moved house.

blocks.prompt: Living in a Borrowed House
blocks.text: Not every hermit crab lives underwater. Walk a beach in Florida or the Caribbean after dark and you may hear a faint scraping in the leaf litter. Those are land hermit crabs, and they have solved a hard problem. They still breathe with gills, and gills only work when they are wet. So a land hermit crab carries a small pool of seawater in the back of its shell, sloshing against its gills with every step. Its house is also its water bottle. The shell does other work too. It keeps the crab from drying out, it hides the soft belly, and it comes with a door. One claw is much larger than the other, and the crab folds that claw across the opening like a shield. Even so, the shell is borrowed. No hermit crab builds one. Every shell it will ever wear was made by a snail that died. Growing is the dangerous part. A hermit crab wears its skeleton on the outside, so to get bigger it has to shed the whole thing. It digs down into damp sand and stays buried for weeks, soft and helpless, while a new skin hardens around it. When it finally climbs out, it eats its old shed skin, because the calcium in it is far too useful to waste. Some ocean hermit crabs hire a bodyguard. They lift a stinging sea anemone onto the roof of their shell and carry it everywhere. The anemone stings anything that comes too close, and in return it gets a free ride and the crumbs from the crab's meals. When the crab moves up to a bigger shell, it reaches back, peels the anemone off carefully, and brings it along.

blocks.prompt: The Housing Market on the Seafloor
blocks.text: Almost every animal that needs armor grows it. The hermit crab does not. Its front end is properly armored, but its abdomen is soft, pale, and coiled into a spiral, which looks like a design mistake until you see what the spiral is for. It matches the inside of a snail shell. The hermit crab reverses into an empty one, hooks its abdomen around the inner column, and carries the shell for the rest of its life. It has outsourced the hardest problem in its body plan to a dead animal. The catch is that a borrowed shell cannot grow. The crab can, and does, so a shell that fit last season becomes a cage the next. Empty shells in good condition are scarce, and a hermit crab that cannot find one will wear a cracked shell, a shell too small to withdraw into, or, increasingly, a plastic bottle cap. Scientists count shells the way economists count housing: as a limited resource that shapes the whole population. What happens when a good shell does appear is one of the strangest things in animal behavior. A crab finds a large empty shell, inspects it, and if the shell is too big, it waits beside it. Another crab arrives and waits too. Crabs keep gathering, and as they gather they arrange themselves into a queue, largest at the front, each one gripping the crab ahead of it, all the way down to the smallest. When the line is long enough, the largest crab moves into the empty shell, and every crab behind it moves up into the shell just abandoned. The whole chain rehouses itself in seconds. Biologists call this a vacancy chain, and the same phrase describes what happens in a human town when one family moves into a new house. One shell arriving on a beach can improve the lives of twenty crabs at once. One shell taken away can leave twenty crabs a size behind.

blocks.prompt: Second Hand: The Animal That Never Built Its Own Armor
blocks.text: Evolution is often described as an arms race, and the sea is full of the evidence: the lobster's plate armor, the clam's hinged fortress, the urchin's spines. The hermit crab entered that race and quietly refused to compete. It grew a hard head and thorax, then stopped, leaving its abdomen soft, pale, and twisted into a right-handed spiral. On its own, that abdomen is an invitation. Paired with an empty snail shell, it is a lock. The spiral of the body matches the spiral of the shell so exactly that the crab can hook itself around the inner column and hold on hard enough to be torn apart before it is pulled out. This is the hermit crab's whole strategy: let a snail spend its life manufacturing calcium carbonate, wait for the snail to die, and move in. Biologists are careful to point out that hermit crabs are not true crabs at all. They sit in a group called the anomurans, closer cousins to squat lobsters, and the borrowed shell is the reason their body plan looks nothing like a blue crab's. The strategy is brilliant and it has one obvious flaw. A shell does not grow. The animal inside it does. A hermit crab must therefore rehouse itself repeatedly across a life that can run past thirty years, and suitable empty shells are one of the scarcest resources on a shoreline. A crab that cannot upgrade will wear a shell it can no longer withdraw into, or a shell with a hole in it, or a plastic bottle cap, and its odds fall accordingly. Researchers study shell supply the way economists study housing stock, because in both cases the supply, not the desire, sets the ceiling. This is where the hermit crab does something that reads more like sociology than zoology. When a large empty shell washes up, the first crab to reach it inspects the shell, and if it is too big, the crab does not leave. It waits. A second crab arrives and waits behind the first. More arrive, and the group sorts itself into a descending queue by size, each crab gripping the shell of the one ahead, sometimes twenty deep. Nothing happens for minutes. Then the largest crab steps into the vacant shell, and in the next few seconds every crab in the line moves forward into the shell the crab ahead of it just left. Researchers call this a synchronous vacancy chain, and they borrowed the term from the study of human housing markets, where one new home at the top of a market frees a home for the next family, and so on down. The comparison is not decoration. It is the same mechanism, running in a different species. It also carries an uncomfortable implication. If a single shell can rehouse twenty animals, then a single shell removed from a beach costs twenty animals a size, and beachcombers empty buckets of shells off shorelines every summer without ever seeing the crabs waiting for them. The hermit crab did not choose a fragile strategy. For most of its history, dead snails were the most reliable thing on the seafloor.
